cognate: ON kné 'knee, lap' = Hitt. genu- 'knee, lap' < *ǵónu; ON svefn/sofna = Hitt. šuppariya- 'sleep' < *swep-/*sup-
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes; ON uses 'lay the head in X's knee', Hittite 'in the beloved knees (lap)'
shared_syntax: sleep (verb/noun) + locative 'in the knee(s)/lap' of a companion
context: a king/god resting before action: Olaf before Stiklestad lays his head in Finnr's knee and sleep comes on him; the Storm-god of Nerik slept sweet sleeps in the beloved knees of his consort Tešimi (Laxdæla has the same ON idiom with a woman's lap). The pair knee+sleep is rare in the index (3 Greek, 2 Germanic, 1 Anatolian units, Greek hits irrelevant).
note: Resting the head in someone's lap is a near-universal image and 'knee' is the natural word for lap in both; ON is late saga prose and in the pivot the lap is a man's. Kept low.

cognate: ON bera = Gk φέρω = Ved. bhṛ- < *bʰer-; ON nafn = Gk ὄνομα = Ved. nā́man- < *h₁nómn̥
drift_or_renewal: Gk middle φέρεσθαι 'carry off (as prize)' vs ON/Ved. active 'bear, hold'
shared_syntax: verb *bʰer- + object *h₁nómn̥ qualified as a name of distinction (ON tígnar nafn 'name of rank'; Gk 'this name' = ὀλβιος; Ved. śrútyam/kīrtényam nā́ma 'famous/praiseworthy name')
context: both passages judge who rightly holds a title of distinction at the end of a life: Erlingr Skjálgsson as the greatest man in Norway who did not bear a higher title (followed by Sigvatr's verse on his death); Solon on who may bear the name 'blessed' after ending life well
note: 'Bear a name' is cross-linguistically common and the inherited name-collocation is rather *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁-; ON and Hdt are prose. Vedic nā́ma bibhr̥- with fame epithets is the strongest support.

near_miss.lead: kinship-term enumerations (father/mother/brother/sister/daughter/son) in Gulaþingslög/Landslög inheritance and killing clauses vs AV/MBh/ORu lists (e.g. drepr faður ... moðor broðor vs mātṛhā pitṛhā svasṛhā)
near_miss.why_not: Cognate kin terms co-occur in any list of relatives; the Norse is legal enumeration of heirs, no shared figure beyond the list itself. The killing-of-kin clause vs AV mātṛhā pitṛhā is closest but still generic.
